comments.author: TekMol
comments.textRawHtml:
Many here call for an earlier release of the patch.

But it is not clear if releasing the fix early would make the damage smaller or larger.

Having the patch probably makes creating an exploit easier. So the number of attacks would increase.

There is no way to coordinate the whole world on an earlier time. I would guess the number of people who have to patch their instances is in the hundreds of thousands.

Everybody who actively watches the topic already has the option to shut down their instances.

So ringing the bell and getting as many people as possible to shut down their webservers now and patch at 14:00 might be the best in terms of damage minimisation.

By the way, it is not enough to just "shutdown -h now" and then later restart and "apt update && apt upgrade". The moment the machine comes back, it can get hacked. So you should make sure the webserver does not start after the next boot. For Apache this would be something like "rm /etc/systemd/system/multi-user.target.wants/apache2.service" and then after patching recreate the symlink via something like "ln -s /lib/systemd/system/apache2.service /etc/systemd/system/multi-user.target.wants/apache2.service".

children.author: overtomanu
children.textRawHtml:
It was "multiple human errors". But yeah no matter what, in any case or exceptional circumstances, this thing was not supposed to be screwed up.

On Mozilla’s tracker, eMudhra said the keys were created on 30 April 2025 in a key generation ceremony, a recorded procedure in which keys are produced inside hardware security modules (HSMs), tamper-resistant devices built to hold keys. The keys were meant to be moved to data centres in the United States and Europe for customers needing data stored in those regions. To move them, the company added a step to ‘wrap’ each key, or encrypt it for transfer, and ‘unwrap’ it at the other end. eMudhra said a flaw in the software script created a second, weaker set of keys during this step, and because the two sets had similar names, staff used the weaker ones by mistake. It said human errors occurred at multiple steps.

children.author: ChuckSneed
children.textRawHtml:
> worked around these types of devices and their interfaces..

This is not a problem of devices and interfaces. You are supposed to generate the wrapping key on the HSM itself. And the HSM ensures that the keys are generated with a strong enough security parameter, not some silly 1 byte string. Then the HSM wraps the key inside of itself and exports it in the encrypted form. You take this ciphertext, and the wrapping key and send it over to the other party.

So if they generate the wrapping key with a funny value, that means they didn't use HSM to generate it but their system openssl. But then, HSMs typically don't allow you to export private keys without wrapping them first unless you first tweak around with security flags (not recommended at all), or simply generate the private key using your system openssl too (LMFAO).

comments.author: johnhtodd
comments.textRawHtml:
(context: I'm the CTO of Quad9 and am one of the people dealing with the lawyers)

There is an understandable focus on "how are you going to block French users" when we have also claimed that geoIP blocking is insufficient for selectively denying resolution for certain names - we understand this conflict, but we think it is energy spent in the wrong place.

It is probable that we will use geoIP filters to block French users from our services after November 24. We could apply this same geoIP filter list now to selectively block French users from reaching the sites that we've been told to make unavailable. But this would corrupt our core premise, which is that the DNS is not the right place for this to happen, and if we comply within France to meet the requirement then we accept the worst eventual outcome for users and we still do not have legally perfect coverage. We wish to first remain consistent with our core mission, and secondarily we must remain as close to compliance as we can to the legal constraints put upon us. By accepting the demands for blocking, we would admit that such demands are permissible within our mission - that we will act on behalf of companies (or others) to create ineffective and mis-directed regimes of content constraint.

We would be admitting that we think this solves the problem - it does not. We would be admitting that we will do this for an ever-increasing number of names - we will not. We would be permitting these methods to be applied for more areas of filtering such as moral, religious, social, or political reasons - we must not.

So we accept that there is the possibility that we will have errors in our blockade, but in this case (blocking French users) we maintain consistency with our stated mission of integrity of the DNS. We would rather there be a clear distinction made for users of our services: you get the DNS as you (the user) expects, or if Quad9 is forced to pollute the service with unexpected and arbitrary number of fragmentation demands, then we will not offer the services at all.

The underlying issue is not ONLY that geoIP blocking is ineffective, but that the entire premise of any of these demands is inappropriately applied to DNS recursive resolution providers. We would hope that this discussion continues to be on the most fundamental of the disagreement we have with the outcome in this court case, not on the details of the technical implementation which have yet to be entirely decided and which can be tuned over time.

comments.author: mbgerring
comments.textRawHtml:
I’m 38 years old, and I’ve worked in climate tech for the last 12 years. In my relatively short lifetime, and my relatively short career, I have seen the environment for political action, and funding for climate solutions, fluctuate maybe half a dozen times.

The physics, however, don’t change, and neither does the task in front of us.

I just spent ten months finding a job, the longest and most difficult job search of my career. It was hard because the macro environment is terrible, but also because I insisted on finding a role working on clean energy hardware.

At a time when basically all VC funding, and in many ways the entire productive capacity of the economy, is shifting to AI, it would have been smarter in some respects to just pivot to AI. I sat out the crypto bubble too, in which some of my peers made a lot of money by working on projects that were either useless, or straightforward scams.

We crossed the 1.5 degree threshold because the money can’t help itself. The slow, steady work of transitioning away from fossil fuels is never going to be as profitable, as quickly, as the various forms of gambling and addiction that have driven the tech industry for most of my lifetime.

But you, individually, can make the choice to keep your eye on the ball. You can commit to working on this problem until it’s done, no matter what. You can choose to find the others to organize and prepare, so that the ideas closest at hand when the next crisis comes are yours.

It’s the best solution I’ve come up with so far, and in spite of the challenges, it’s still working.

children.author: ButlerianJihad
children.textRawHtml:
In the Phoenix Metro area, the fares are capped, so you never pay beyond the cap for daily, weekly, or monthly fares.

If you ride and pay your fare twice, then every ride after that, for the rest of the day, is free. That is very nice. So if you commute and you have a transfer, and you're taking 4 rides per day, then you're saving half of that in fares.

In the old days, you would pay a cash fare and the bus operator could issue a paper transfer ticket. The transfer would be good for a few hours. So your fare was basically per-trip. But the system couldn't track people paying cash fares like that, so there were no free rides without the transfer ticket. If you took two trips a day, like a normal commute, you'd pay at least two fares. Now, with pre-loaded cards or fares on the mobile app, you can track all that stuff, and reload when necessary.

For disabled people or whoever qualifies for "Reduced Fare", your fare costs half ($1.00 instead of $2.00) and so your daily maximum is only $2.00. A really good deal.

Libraries are free. (Well, at least most public libraries. There are private libraries for personal use, institutional libraries for internal use, subscription libraries which require membership fees, and others.)

I've visited libraries in a half dozen countries, where I'm not even a taxpayer. I just walked in.

Some services at the library might not be free, including book checkout or making photocopies.

But if you want to make that distinction, then walking around your neighborhood isn't free because in most place you need to wear clothes, and clothes aren't free.

FWIW, I've walked a lot of forest roads without a car or bike. And the biggest littering problem on our sidewalks, by weight, are the escooter riders who simply leave their machines parked in the middle of the sidewalk.

The problem isn't that the sidewalks are free to use, the problem is one of regulation and enforcement.

That's why libraries are both free and well-loved - they librarians regulate the free space.

Archive is a nice solution in between just letting it rot on the vine forever and deleting it. Leaving it open doesn't immediately signal to users that the codebase is no longer in development, youd have to check when the last commit was. And even then, that doesn't tell you much. Is this so simple of an app that there's really nothing to patch or upgrade for long periods? A python script that converts some legacy file format into an open one might effectively be complete, there's nothing left to add or fix and there's no real threat vector to exploit. Or is this a cutting edge app that someone committed daily for years but now hasn't moved in a year.

The one thing I don't like about archive is the inability to add new issues. If I encounter a new issue, I don't necessarily want to fork it and track the new issue myself. I don't want to take responsibility for the code, I just want to let people know so someone else can fix it if they care.

children.author: dlcarrier
children.textRawHtml:
The optimal airport has two parallel runways, 9,000 feet apart, that align with prevailing wind. If a location has variable strong winds, another set can be built at a 90° angle. It's possible to add more runways at 9,000 intervals, but you're usually better off building an airport somewhere else.

Most airports were built during or before WWII, so few are designed to most efficiently accommodate modern usage. Maybe in the future we can better handle closer runways in low visibility, but first we'll have to figure out how to have two computers communicate directly with each other, instead of having one computer generate routes that get read out load by a human, transmitted over an analog radio, listened to by another human, then typed into another computer.

That just makes it computer -> person -> computer -> computer -> person -> computer

We need something where a control center computer that issues clearances can radio them directly into an aircraft's flight management computer. This wouldn't disallow ATC from reviewing the routes before transmitting them, or the flight crew from reviewing them before accepting them, but without people manually copying over the information, there's a lot less potential to insert errors in the first place.
